stories.headline: US jobs market sees sharp slowdown ahead of midterm elections

claims.text: The US economy added just 29,000 jobs in September.
The US economy added a revised 133,000 jobs in August.
The unemployment rate rose from 4.1% in August to 4.2% in September.
This was the final BLS jobs report released before the US midterm congressional elections.
An AP/NORC poll released the same week found only 17% of Americans approve of President Trump's handling of cost-of-living issues.
An AP/NORC poll released the same week found 26% of Americans approve of President Trump's handling of the economy overall.
Those approval figures are described as new lows for Trump.
Those approval figures are lower than Joe Biden's lowest marks during his presidency.
Economists cited include George Brown of Schroders, Bradley Saunders of Capital Economics, and Jeffery Roach of LPL Financial.
Trump said at a White House event, 'I've done a very bad job of explaining how good the country is doing.'
The September jobs report shows a sharp deceleration in hiring compared with August.
The September jobs report shows a slight uptick in unemployment.
This is the last major labor-market data release before the midterm elections.
Weaker job growth generally reduces pressure for further interest-rate increases.
Multiple economists highlighted that weaker job growth reduces pressure for further interest-rate increases.
The data arrives alongside polling showing historically low public approval of the president's economic stewardship.
There is a visible gap between official White House messaging about a 'booming' economy and both the BLS figures and public sentiment.
Economists across differing institutions converge on a similar read: this single report, while weak, is not evidence of economic collapse.
The report will likely factor into the Federal Reserve's near-term interest-rate deliberations.
Economists suggest the report lowers the odds of additional interest-rate hikes.
The report sets the economic backdrop for the final weeks of midterm campaigning.
Both the jobs data and approval polling may shape voter perceptions of the administration's economic record.

facts: The US economy added just 29,000 jobs in September, down from a revised 133,000 in August, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics.
The unemployment rate rose from 4.1% in August to 4.2% in September.
This was the final BLS jobs report released before the US midterm congressional elections.
An AP/NORC poll released the same week found only 17% of Americans approve of President Trump's handling of cost-of-living issues and 26% approve of his handling of the economy overall.
Those approval figures are described as new lows for Trump, lower than Joe Biden's lowest marks during his presidency.
Economists cited include George Brown of Schroders, Bradley Saunders of Capital Economics, and Jeffery Roach of LPL Financial, who offered differing assessments of the report's severity.
Trump said at a White House event, "I've done a very bad job of explaining how good the country is doing."
ladder.analysis: The September jobs report shows a sharp deceleration in hiring compared with August, alongside a slight uptick in unemployment. Because this is the last major labor-market data release before the midterm elections, it carries added political weight, landing just as voters are forming views on economic conditions. The slowdown also has direct bearing on Federal Reserve policy: weaker job growth generally reduces pressure for further interest-rate increases, a point multiple economists highlighted. The data arrives alongside polling showing historically low public approval of the president's economic stewardship, creating a visible gap between official White House messaging about a "booming" economy and both the BLS figures and public sentiment.
ladder.steelman: Economists across differing institutions converge on a similar read: this single report, while weak, is not evidence of economic collapse, but it does sit awkwardly alongside polling showing record-low public confidence in the administration's economic management—underscoring a genuine gap between official messaging and both the data and public perception, independent of partisan framing.
ladder.implications: The report will likely factor into the Federal Reserve's near-term interest-rate deliberations, with economists suggesting it lowers the odds of additional hikes. It also sets the economic backdrop for the final weeks of midterm campaigning, during which both the jobs data and approval polling may shape voter perceptions of the administration's economic record.

stories.headline: Cornell rape case: Hochul calls probe a failure, students voice anger

spectrum.tilt_pill: Coverage is balanced across the spectrum

claims.text: Jane Doe filed a civil lawsuit against Cornell University on Sept. 16.
Jane Doe alleged she was drugged and gang-raped by multiple fraternity members at a Chi Phi house in October 2024.
The men involved have been dubbed the 'Cornell Seven.'
Cornell says its original investigation, lasting several months, resulted in a 'range of sanctions' including expulsions and suspensions.
The civil complaint states some students who received temporary suspensions were offered the option to submit essays to mitigate their conduct.
Tompkins County DA Matthew Van Houten said his office reviewed Doe's November 2024 sworn statement and initially found the facts did not support criminal charges.
Van Houten described the statement as portraying the conduct as voluntary.
Van Houten's office reopened a criminal investigation last week after the civil complaint was filed.
Cornell supported the reopening of the criminal investigation.
Gov. Kathy Hochul appointed state Attorney General Letitia James as special prosecutor on the case.
Hochul said she had 'lost faith' in Van Houten.
Hochul called Cornell's handling of the incident 'a failure.'
Hochul stopped short of calling for the resignation of Cornell's president or Van Houten.
Cornell closed its Chi Phi fraternity chapter in 2024.
Chi Phi remains barred from campus.
Cornell says it is legally restricted from publicly disclosing specific disciplinary outcomes.
More than 1,300 Cornell alumni signed a letter published in the student newspaper calling for 'swift and expansive' action from the university.
Students held a public assembly on campus Thursday to voice anger over the case.
A 'Justice for Survivors' protest is planned for Oct. 5.
Organizers of the protest are demanding expulsions, policy changes, an external investigation and mandatory prevention training.
Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez said at a Sept. 28 town hall that 'seven men drugged and gang raped' Doe for seven hours.
Ocasio-Cortez said that Cornell's punishment amounted to having some students 'write essays.'
Cornell disputed Ocasio-Cortez's characterization, saying expulsions and suspensions were issued and no respondent's sole punishment was an essay.

facts: Jane Doe filed a civil lawsuit against Cornell University on Sept. 16, alleging she was drugged and gang-raped by multiple fraternity members at a Chi Phi house in October 2024; the men involved have been dubbed the 'Cornell Seven.'

Cornell says its original investigation, lasting several months, resulted in a 'range of sanctions' including expulsions and suspensions; the civil complaint states some students who received temporary suspensions were offered the option to submit essays to mitigate their conduct.

Tompkins County DA Matthew Van Houten said his office reviewed Doe's November 2024 sworn statement and initially found the facts did not support criminal charges, describing the statement as portraying the conduct as voluntary; his office reopened a criminal investigation last week after the civil complaint was filed, a move Cornell supported.

Gov. Kathy Hochul (D-NY) appointed state Attorney General Letitia James as special prosecutor on the case, saying she had 'lost faith' in Van Houten, and called Cornell's handling of the incident 'a failure,' but stopped short of calling for the resignation of Cornell's president or Van Houten.
Cornell closed its Chi Phi fraternity chapter in 2024, and it remains barred from campus; the university says it is legally restricted from publicly disclosing specific disciplinary outcomes.
More than 1,300 Cornell alumni signed a letter published in the student newspaper calling for 'swift and expansive' action from the university.

Students held a public assembly on campus Thursday to voice anger over the case, and a 'Justice for Survivors' protest is planned for Oct. 5, with organizers demanding expulsions, policy changes, an external investigation and mandatory prevention training.

Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-NY) said at a Sept. 28 town hall that 'seven men drugged and gang raped' Doe for seven hours and that Cornell's punishment amounted to having some students 'write essays'; Cornell disputed this characterization, saying expulsions and suspensions were issued and no respondent's sole punishment was an essay.
ladder.analysis: The case centers on a 2024 alleged gang rape at a Cornell fraternity that resurfaced publicly after the accuser, known as Jane Doe, filed a civil lawsuit accusing the university of inadequately protecting or punishing those involved. The controversy has unfolded on two tracks: a legal one, where the local prosecutor first declined charges based on an earlier statement from Doe but has since reopened the criminal investigation, and a political/institutional one, where New York's governor replaced the local DA with the state attorney general and publicly faulted Cornell's handling of the matter without calling for anyone's ouster. Simultaneously, the case has become a flashpoint on campus and in wider political discourse, with student groups, faculty and alumni demanding transparency and reform, and a prominent member of Congress offering a dramatic public account of the allegations that Cornell disputes in part.
ladder.steelman: Beyond the competing factual narratives, the episode highlights a recurring tension in high-profile campus assault cases between legal processes (which hinge on specific statements and evidentiary thresholds) and public/political narratives (which can amplify or compress details for advocacy purposes) — both of which readers must track separately to understand what is proven, alleged, or disputed.
ladder.implications: The outcome will likely hinge on two parallel processes: the reopened criminal investigation now under Attorney General Letitia James, and Cornell's agreed-upon independent review of its handling of the case. Continued student protests, alumni pressure, and political scrutiny suggest the university's leadership and disciplinary policies will remain under close watch, with potential consequences for Cornell's administration, the fraternity system, and possibly new state-level scrutiny of how colleges handle sexual assault complaints.

stories.headline: G7 to release 100M barrels of fuel as Trump threatens diesel export ban

claims.text: The G7 consists of Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan, the UK and the US.
The G7 said Friday it will "begin immediately" releasing 100 million barrels of fuel, including diesel, from stockpiles over the next four months.
UK diesel pump prices hit a record high this week.
UK diesel pump prices averaged 199.79p per litre this week, according to the RAC.
UK diesel pump prices previously averaged 142.38p per litre, according to the RAC.
President Trump said he is considering a ban on US diesel exports.
President Trump said he "may" ask European countries to release some of their own diesel reserves.
The US exports between 1.2 and 1.5 million barrels of diesel per day.
Most US diesel exports go to Latin America.
European buyers including France, the Netherlands and the UK import US diesel.
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent posted that Europe should prepare to release diesel supplies.
Scott Bessent posted that US farmers, truckers and businesses "should not be left carrying the burden" of rising prices.
UK Energy Minister Martin McCluskey held a call with European counterparts on Thursday.
The UK said it had been discussing the US supply threats with the EU.
The EU was due to hold a meeting Friday on the issue.
Under IEA rules, the UK must hold oil stocks equal to 90 days of net imports.
Under EU rules, EU members must hold reserves covering 61 days of consumption.
The EU holds roughly 109 million tons of emergency crude and fuel stocks.
About a third of the EU's emergency crude and fuel stocks is diesel-related.
Contributing factors cited for the price spike include the US-Israel war with Iran affecting the Strait of Hormuz.
Contributing factors cited for the price spike include Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries.
Contributing factors cited for the price spike include a Russian diesel export ban.
Contributing factors cited for the price spike include China halting some October fuel exports.
Diesel prices have surged globally due to a combination of disruptions.
The war involving the US, Israel and Iran has constrained flows through the Strait of Hormuz.
The Strait of Hormuz normally carries about a fifth of the world's oil and gas.
Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries have removed a major source of diesel from international markets.
A Russian export ban has removed another major source of diesel from international markets.
Chinese refiners have reportedly cut back on fuel exports to prioritize domestic supply.
A US diesel export ban could lower domestic pump prices ahead of November midterms by keeping more US-refined diesel at home.
The US is a key supplier of diesel to Europe and Latin America.
Officials in the UK and EU have been in contact over the issue.
Experts such as Argus Media's David Fyfe have warned that cutting off US diesel supply would likely cause international prices to skyrocket.
The UK relies heavily on US diesel imports.
The UK government has said it continues to engage with international partners and the UK fuel industry.
The UK government has stressed there is no cause for concern about diesel shortages.

facts: The G7 (Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan, UK, US) said Friday it will "begin immediately" releasing 100 million barrels of fuel, including diesel, from stockpiles over the next four months.
UK diesel pump prices hit a record high this week, averaging 199.79p per litre according to the RAC, up from 142.38p previously.
President Trump said he is considering a ban on US diesel exports and said he "may" ask European countries to release some of their own diesel reserves.
The US exports between 1.2 and 1.5 million barrels of diesel per day, with most going to Latin America; European buyers including France, the Netherlands and the UK also import US diesel.
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent posted that Europe should prepare to release diesel supplies so that US farmers, truckers and businesses "should not be left carrying the burden" of rising prices.

UK Energy Minister Martin McCluskey held a call with European counterparts on Thursday, and the UK said it had been discussing the US supply threats with the EU, which was due to hold a meeting Friday on the issue.

Under IEA rules the UK must hold oil stocks equal to 90 days of net imports, and under EU rules members must hold reserves covering 61 days of consumption; the EU holds roughly 109 million tons of emergency crude and fuel stocks, about a third of it diesel-related.

Contributing factors cited for the price spike include the US-Israel war with Iran affecting the Strait of Hormuz, Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries, a Russian diesel export ban, and China halting some October fuel exports.
ladder.analysis:
Diesel prices have surged globally due to a combination of disruptions: the war involving the US, Israel and Iran has constrained flows through the Strait of Hormuz, which normally carries about a fifth of the world's oil and gas; Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries and a Russian export ban have removed another major source of diesel from international markets; and Chinese refiners have reportedly cut back on fuel exports to prioritize domestic supply. Against this backdrop, the G7 said it would release 100 million barrels of fuel, including diesel, from stockpiles over the next four months.

Separately, Trump is considering a US diesel export ban, which could lower domestic pump prices ahead of the November midterms by keeping more US-refined diesel at home. But since the US exports 1.2-1.5 million barrels a day and is a key supplier to Europe and Latin America, officials in the UK and EU have been in contact over the issue, including a call between the UK energy minister and European counterparts and a planned EU meeting on the matter.
ladder.steelman: The underlying tension in this story is structural, not partisan: a US export ban could offer relief to American drivers and businesses before the midterms, but experts such as Argus Media's David Fyfe have warned that cutting off US diesel supply would likely cause international prices to skyrocket, which would be felt by countries like the UK that rely heavily on US diesel imports.
ladder.implications: The G7's 100-million-barrel fuel release is scheduled to unfold over the next four months. The UK government has said it continues to engage with international partners and the UK fuel industry, and has stressed there is no cause for concern about diesel shortages, though it expects prices to rise further.

stories.headline: US sends third aircraft carrier and thousands more troops to Middle East amid Iran war
body: The United States is sending a third aircraft carrier and thousands more troops to the Middle East, a U.S. official confirmed Thursday, as President Donald Trump vowed that the seven-month war with Iran would end "right after the election" or sooner. The USS Theodore Roosevelt Carrier Strike Group and the USS Makin Island Amphibious Group are heading to the region, adding roughly 10,000 sailors and Marines, according to U.S. officials. The deployment brings total U.S. forces in the region to approximately 20,000, along with hundreds of vessels and aircraft, with the USS George Washington and USS Boxer already operating there.

Speaking at a rally in Denton, Texas, Trump said Iran "is ready to fold up" and that the U.S. would win the war "right after the election—but maybe before the election." He claimed Iran's leaders are "gone," that its navy is at the bottom of the sea, and that its missile manufacturing capacity is "dead." Trump also said Iran was "3 to 4 weeks away" from acquiring a nuclear weapon before the war began, and that energy prices, which have soared during the conflict, would come "pouring down" once the war ends. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent announced that Iran did not load a single barrel of crude oil onto tankers in September, calling the milestone part of "Operation Economic Outcast."

The deployment comes as oil prices surged more than $4 a barrel amid concerns about regional stability. The Saudi-led coalition fighting Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis accused the rebels of attacking an electricity distribution station in the Saudi city of Medina, home to the second holiest site in Islam, drawing condemnation across the Muslim world. Intense fighting between Houthi and Saudi-backed forces near the Red Sea killed 80 combatants over the past day, according to sources on both sides. The United Nations Population Fund said hostilities in Yemen have displaced more than 145,000 people, including 35,000 women of childbearing age and more than 3,200 pregnant women, with some giving birth on the roadside while fleeing.

President Trump suggested Iran could be linked to an alleged attempted hijacking of an Israel-bound FlyDubai flight, in which the co-pilot reportedly stabbed the captain and tried to crash the plane with 174 people on board. Asked if Iran's Revolutionary Guard Corps was involved, Trump said "he could've been, yeah," adding that "they'll be hit, very hard, don't worry." Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said authorities were investigating whether the co-pilot was "dispatched" by a third party. In a separate development, the Justice Department charged Ashton Hamed Ellaboudy, 51, a Department of Energy employee from Richland, Washington, with attempting to provide material support to the Houthis, alleging he helped test and modify solar generators and communications equipment for an undercover FBI source posing as a Houthi representative.

European Union nations have discussed a French proposal to release 50 million barrels of diesel from reserves, a source told Reuters, amid U.S. pressure to ease fuel prices. The discussions included a demand that the U.S. not unilaterally ban diesel exports. Russian President Vladimir Putin said he hopes the Strait of Hormuz remains open to shipping and that Moscow could help remove Iran's enriched uranium. Iran's parliament has completed a committee-level consideration of a proposed bill that would establish what lawmakers frame as the future Iranian management of the Strait of Hormuz, including the imposition of fees on commercial vessels using the vital waterway, according to the semi-official Tasnim news agency. The Trump administration rejects Iran's demands for all commercial vessels to seek permission for transits, and Iran has repeatedly targeted tankers in the waterway since the war began.

Lebanese Prime Minister Nawaf Salam said his country cannot rebuild from the latest Israel-Hezbollah war alone, saying "the scale of the needs exceeds the capacities of the Lebanese state." Lebanese authorities have put the overall death toll from both rounds of fighting at more than 8,900, with hundreds of thousands of people displaced, mainly from the south. Iraqi Ambassador to Tehran Yasser Abdul Zahra Al-Hajjaj said flights between Iran and Iraq will resume soon, as the two countries work to resolve disruptions to air travel. The U.S. Central Command released video of the USS George Washington conducting flight operations in the Middle East, signaling its presence amid the Iranian port blockade.

stories.headline: Russian strikes paralyze Kyiv bridges, kill one as mayor warns city is being 'torn apart'
stories.byline: International & World desk · anchored on Reuters
body: Russian drone and missile strikes have intensified on Kyiv, killing at least one person and forcing the closure of three major bridges over the Dnipro River, Kyiv Mayor Vitaliy Klitschko said Friday. The attacks, which included repeated strikes on the Pivdennyi (Southern) Bridge — hit four times in two days — have caused traffic gridlock across the Ukrainian capital. Klitschko warned that the strikes were "tearing Kyiv apart" and described the situation as "very dramatic," with critical infrastructure, logistics, and housing under sustained assault.

The Southern Bridge, a key transport artery connecting western and eastern Kyiv, was struck overnight and again Friday evening, suspending all metro and automobile traffic. The Paton Bridge was closed toward the left bank, and the Metro Bridge was shut in the direction of the right bank, the city administration said. One person was killed when a multi-story residential building in the Darnytskyi district was hit, Ukraine's State Emergency Service reported. At least two others were injured. Kyiv's data centers have also been targeted in recent days, causing internet outages. The city's population is estimated at about three million, many of whom rely on the metro network.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said the attacks reflect a decision by Russian President Vladimir Putin in early September that "there are no rules now." In an interview with the Financial Times, Zelensky said: "The Russians have failed to occupy us. So now they are carrying out massive attacks and mass killings. They want to destroy our bridges... our data centres, the internet, mobile networks, hospitals, kindergartens, schools, universities — everything. They want people to flee their cities." Zelensky called on allies to tighten sanctions against Russia, arguing that Moscow remains dependent on foreign components for its drones and missiles, and that supply chains run through Europe, the United States, China, and Japan.

Russian President Vladimir Putin, speaking Thursday at the Valdai foreign policy forum, insisted the strikes on Ukrainian economic targets were a direct response to Ukraine's attacks on Russian oil refineries and Black Sea ships. "Now from every direction we're receiving calls 'let's stop'. But they started it," Putin said. He acknowledged that Ukraine had "got some results" from its refinery attacks and that Russia had lost about 1% of its GDP. Ukraine maintains it targets Russian oil infrastructure because it helps finance the war. Russia has ramped up strikes on Ukrainian energy infrastructure every winter since launching its full-scale invasion in 2022.

Elsewhere in Ukraine, Russian strikes hit a kindergarten in Kherson, a grocery store in Kharkiv, and apartment buildings in Kramatorsk and Sumy, Zelensky said. The Dnipro, Odesa, Kharkiv, Kyiv, Poltava, and Rivne regions also came under attack, with at least four people reported wounded. Russia's Defense Ministry said its drones struck a bridge over the Dnipro used for military purposes, a power station in the Kyiv region, the Izmail port near Odesa, and a cargo vessel. Ukraine's military carried out its own overnight attacks on Russia, hitting a Lukoil facility in Volgograd and an oil dispatch station in the Samara region, causing fires. Ukrainian forces also targeted airfields and industrial sites in several Russian regions, including in the Black Sea, Zelensky said. Russian authorities in the Black Sea port town of Tuapse reported damage to an enterprise from drone debris.

stories.headline: Ethiopia and Eritrea sever diplomatic ties as northern fighting intensifies
body: Ethiopia and Eritrea have severed diplomatic relations, marking a dramatic reversal of the rapprochement that won Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed the Nobel Peace Prize in 2019. On Thursday, Ethiopia announced it was closing its embassy in the Eritrean capital, Asmara, and ordered 10 Eritrean diplomats to leave the country within 48 hours, accusing them of activities that threatened national security. Eritrea responded by cutting diplomatic ties, saying Ethiopia's decision left it with no choice but to take reciprocal action.

The diplomatic confrontation came hours after powerful explosions were heard overnight in the Ethiopian capital, Addis Ababa, including near Ethiopia's military headquarters. AFP quoted a diplomatic source as saying small drones were the most probable cause of the blast. The fighting in northern Ethiopia is the most serious since a peace agreement ended the devastating Tigray war in 2022. An African Union mediator previously estimated that about 600,000 people had died during that two-year conflict.

The latest hostilities involve Ethiopian federal forces battling fighters from the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF) and its allies across parts of the northern regions of Tigray, Afar and Amhara. Last month, the TPLF joined six other armed movements, including the Fano militia from Amhara, to form an alliance whose stated objective is to remove Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed's government from power. Federal forces and their allies appear to have made gains in southern Tigray and are advancing towards the regional capital, Mekelle. In Alamata, a doctor told the BBC earlier this week that at least 52 civilians had been killed during three days of intense fighting.

Ethiopia has accused Eritrea of supporting the new rebel alliance — an allegation Asmara has repeatedly denied. In a rare response before diplomatic relations were severed, Eritrea's Information Minister Yemane Gebremeskel told BBC Tigrinya that Ethiopia's governing Prosperity Party was blaming neighbouring countries to divert attention from conflicts and other problems within Ethiopia. A pro-government militia commander fighting in Tigray told the BBC that Eritrean soldiers had been involved on the front lines, but the BBC has not independently verified the allegation. The BBC is unable to report from Tigray and the internet and phone lines have been cut, making it difficult to get reliable information from the region.

The cutting of ties between Ethiopia and Eritrea mark a dramatic reversal from 2018, when Abiy restored relations with Asmara after two decades of hostility, prompting joyous scenes as the border reopened and families separated for years were reunited. Relations have deteriorated significantly since then, particularly over Ethiopia's push for direct access to the Red Sea. Ethiopia lost its coastline when Eritrea became independent in 1993. Abiy has repeatedly argued that access to the sea is essential to Ethiopia's long-term economic and security interests, while Eritrea has accused his government of harbouring ambitions over its ports.

Ethiopia has also expelled an Egyptian diplomat, giving him 48 hours to leave the country, according to state media. Egypt responded by ordering an Ethiopian embassy official to leave within the same period, according to the state-affiliated Al Qahera News. Relations between Ethiopia and Egypt have been strained for years, largely over Ethiopia's Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam (GERD), a huge hydroelectric project on the Blue Nile. Egypt, which relies heavily on the Nile for its water supplies, has long expressed concern about the dam's potential impact on its share of the river's water. The African Union has urged Ethiopia, Eritrea and Egypt to exercise restraint and resolve their differences through diplomatic channels, warning against actions that could further destabilise the region. The UN has also warned that the deteriorating security situation is severely disrupting humanitarian work in northern Ethiopia, with drone activity and air strikes putting civilians, vital infrastructure and aid operations at risk.

stories.headline: G7 announces 100-million-barrel oil reserve release; Trump hails Europe diesel deal
body: The Group of Seven (G7) announced Friday it will release up to 100 million barrels of oil from strategic reserves over four months in a coordinated effort to curb soaring energy prices driven by the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran. The release, to be conducted through the International Energy Agency (IEA), includes a "frontloaded substantial diesel release within the first 20 days by G7 members and partners," according to a statement following a meeting chaired by French President Emmanuel Macron. The group said it will convene under the IEA in the coming days to discuss the possibility of additional diesel releases as necessary.

The announcement came shortly after U.S. President Donald Trump posted on his Truth Social account that Europe "just agreed to release a massive amount of their heavily stocked Diesel Oil." Trump had pressured European countries, notably Germany and France, to release diesel stockpiles to ease soaring prices caused by shipping disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz, a consequence of the war with Iran that began on February 28. The White House official told Al Jazeera that the U.S. is "tight on diesel" due to lost exports from Russia, the Middle East, and China, adding that American refiners are running at record highs.

EU countries, along with the United Kingdom, hold approximately 52 million metric tonnes of gas oil and diesel stocks, including nearly 38 million tonnes of emergency reserves, according to Eurostat data from June 2026. EU rules require member states to maintain emergency oil stocks covering at least 90 days of net imports or 61 days of domestic consumption. Germany holds the largest emergency stock at 5.6 million tonnes, followed by France with 8.2 million tonnes. In contrast, U.S. diesel inventories hit a record low of 107.9 million barrels as of September 11, 2026. The national average for a gallon of diesel in the U.S. was $6.37 on Friday, down from a record $6.52 on September 22.

Trump had previously threatened to ban U.S. diesel exports if European countries did not release their stockpiles. The EU rejected that threat on Friday, with EU trade chief Maros Sefcovic telling reporters after a G-20 trade meeting that he had discussed tight diesel supplies with U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer and expressed Europe's desire for a coordinated approach to lowering prices. An EU government official told Politico that the Trump administration sent a proposal to EU leaders on Thursday asking them to release 120 million barrels of diesel over 180 days. On Friday, the EU's energy task force met to discuss a French proposal under which European countries would release 50 million barrels of diesel and IEA members would release 50 million barrels of crude oil.

Relations between the U.S. and EU have been tense since Trump imposed new tariffs on the bloc last year and demanded a deal to buy Greenland, which led European nations to send troops to the island in a show of defiance. Ties have further soured as EU nations refused to allow the U.S. to use their airbases for attacks on Iran. Frederic Schneider, a nonresident senior fellow at the Middle East Council on Global Affairs, told Al Jazeera that while Europe holds large mandatory product stocks, "the Trumpian fashion of issuing every request as an ultimatum makes it harder for European governments to agree." He predicted Europe would give some ground through an IEA-coordinated release "well short of 120 million barrels" to avoid being perceived as capitulating to Washington.

The issue has been politically damaging for Trump and his Republican Party ahead of the November midterm elections, with Trump's approval on the economy plunging. High global energy prices have been a knock-on effect of the war with Iran, which Trump launched alongside Israel on February 28. In March, the IEA's 32 member countries agreed to unlock 400 million barrels of oil from emergency reserves, though officials said that release has not yet been fully completed. The G7 includes Canada, France, Germany, Italy, the United Kingdom, and the United States, with the European Union as an observer member.

stories.headline: September Jobs Miss Crushes Fed October Rate-Hike Odds; Stocks, Bonds Rally
stories.byline: Financial & Markets desk · anchored on Reuters
body: The U.S. economy added just 29,000 jobs in September, far below the 84,000 expected by economists, while the unemployment rate rose to 4.2%, the Bureau of Labor Statistics reported Friday. The weak reading sent stock and bond markets rallying as traders slashed bets that the Federal Reserve will raise interest rates at its October meeting. The Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 0.6%, the S&P 500 gained 1%, and the Nasdaq Composite surged 1.7%, hitting a record high. The 10-year Treasury yield fell to 5.21%, and the 30-year yield dropped to 5.57%.

Market-implied odds of a quarter-point rate hike at the Fed's Oct. 27-28 meeting collapsed to about 17% on the CME Group's FedWatch tool, down from roughly 36% a week earlier. On the prediction market Kalshi, October hike odds fell to 18% from nearly 70% a week ago. "For the Fed, this number should be the nail in the coffin for an October hike," said Thomas Simons, chief U.S. economist at Jefferies. The August jobs count was revised lower to 133,000, and July was revised from a gain to a loss of 10,000, for a net downward revision of 60,000 jobs.

Average hourly earnings rose just 0.1% in September, bringing the 12-month gain to 3% — the lowest since May 2021 and below the 3.1% expected. The average work week held steady at 34.6 hours. "Americans are frustrated by the lack of opportunities right now," said Heather Long, chief economist at Navy Federal Credit Union. "Wage growth fell to a new 5-year low and is being wiped out entirely by inflation. That stings heading into the holidays." The household survey showed a brighter picture: employment rose by 406,000, the labor force swelled by 485,000, and the participation rate climbed to 61.8%, its highest since May. An alternative measure of unemployment that includes discouraged workers and those working part-time for economic reasons edged down to 7.6%, its lowest since January 2025.

Most job gains came from healthcare, which added 17,000 workers; construction rose by 11,000, and manufacturing added 9,000. Government employment fell by 17,000, temporary help services lost 11,000, information services shed 10,000 amid concerns about artificial intelligence's impact, and financial activities dropped 7,000. Despite the weak payrolls number, broader economic growth has been strong: the Commerce Department revised first-quarter GDP to 2.5% and second-quarter GDP to 2.2%, and the Atlanta Fed is tracking third-quarter GDP at 3.7%.

The report comes as Fed officials weigh the state of the economy and inflation, which has held well above the central bank's 2% target. The Fed's preferred inflation gauge, the core personal consumption expenditures price index, rose 3% in August, lighter than the 3.3% consensus. "This report strengthens the case for the Federal Reserve to remain patient," said Adam Schickling, a senior economist at Vanguard. "The labor market has not deteriorated sharply, but there is also little evidence that it has meaningfully strengthened, giving policymakers reason to wait for additional data." While October hike odds have collapsed, traders still see a greater than 75% chance of a rate increase in December on FedWatch and 65% odds on Kalshi. Brent crude futures fell to $99 per barrel on Friday.

stories.headline: AI 'Agent Orchestration' Demand Surges 1,721% as Banks Hire for New Wall Street Skill
body: Demand for a new AI skill set is exploding on Wall Street. References to 'agent orchestration'—the ability to design multiple AI agents that work together on a task—jumped 1,721% this year, according to an analysis by enterprise hiring data firm Draup provided exclusively to CNBC. The surge comes as major banks including JPMorgan Chase, Citigroup and Capital One have posted 139,819 AI-related roles this year, a 49% increase compared with 2025.

Draup CEO Vijay Swaminathan called agent orchestration 'arguably the hottest skill on Wall Street,' describing it as 'a massive opportunity.' The workers who fill these roles, often called forward-deployed engineers, must combine technical abilities with deep knowledge of a specific business function—from trading desks to back-office operations and human resources. Their job is to determine which agents are needed, what each one does, which technology to use, and when human oversight is required. 'There is a lot of complexity in an enterprise,' Swaminathan said. 'Sometimes these complexities are visible, but many times they are hidden. It takes a long time even to automate a simple process.'

The shift reflects banks moving beyond chatbots into a next-phase AI strategy that relies on armies of specialized agents handling an increasing share of labor. Deploying AI inside a financial institution often means stringing together multiple agents: one to inspect raw data, another to analyze a document, and a third to check regulatory compliance. Other in-demand skills tied to this build-out include LangGraph (references up 679%), LlamaIndex (up 291%), and retrieval-augmented generation, or RAG (up 259%).

Beyond technical expertise, Draup's analysis shows a renewed emphasis on soft skills such as problem solving, creativity, the ability to ask tough questions, and assertiveness in understanding processes. At the same time, demand is rising for roles that create guardrails around AI systems. References to 'responsible AI' surged 657%, while mentions of AI governance and risk management jumped 394% and 359%, respectively. Governance-related skills now account for more than 16,000 references in Draup's data, nearly double the roughly 8,400 references tied to training, deploying and running models. Swaminathan noted a strong focus on ensuring that third-party tools and external model connections do not create systemic cybersecurity vulnerabilities.

Roles tied to generative AI and agents typically command higher pay than other tech roles in finance, with generative AI managers earning a median base salary of about $190,000, according to Draup. Despite the premium, filling these specialized positions remains a challenge. To bridge the gap, major banks are leaning heavily into internal reskilling programs to train existing developers and domain experts. The build-out is expected to create ripple effects: JPMorgan CEO Jamie Dimon has spoken of 'huge redeployment plans' as AI takes over more work. 'I think the more we prioritize those soft skills with the right amount of technical skills, people will adapt and learn,' Swaminathan said. 'It's a very exciting time for the right talent.'

stories.headline: Man City confirm appeal against guilty financial verdict
body: Manchester City have lodged an appeal against an independent commission's guilty verdict on all charges relating to breaches of the Premier League's financial regulations between 2009-10 and 2017-18, calling the ruling "unsafe" and containing "clear material errors, of law, principle and fact." The club submitted its appeal on Thursday evening and said "a comprehensive body of irrefutable evidence" supports its positions.

The commission found City "utilised devices" to disguise the true extent of certain club liabilities, including arranging "sham contracts" with commercial partners as part of a scheme to hide more than £830m in secret funding. The Premier League says City "systematically broke Premier League Rules for nearly a decade." It is understood City will argue in their appeal that key sponsorship deals were funded by the Abu Dhabi government rather than the club's owners, Abu Dhabi United Group, which is said to have topped up commercial deals to make the club appear compliant with financial rules.

The Football Association said the verdict has "significant implications for the integrity of the game" and it is "carefully considering the decision and its implications and will take action where appropriate," though it declined further comment while proceedings remain ongoing. Separately, the Treasury Committee has asked HMRC whether it has requested the redacted documents from the commission's report, following a report claiming City failed to pay as much as £12m in unpaid tax because of a "sham" contract with former manager Roberto Mancini, potentially rising to £24m with penalties. City's principal sponsor Etihad Airways, which said it was not named in the published findings, is considering legal action over the "damaging implications" of the release.

The appeal will be heard in private by a new, three-person independent commission panel. Under Premier League regulations introduced this summer, an appeal hearing should conclude within 12 weeks — 24 December if calculated from Thursday — with a decision communicated within 30 days, though the timeframe can be disapplied. Previous precedent suggests sanctions against City will only be imposed after a decision on the appeal, and a second appeal against any sanctions remains possible.

The verdict has created significant uncertainty over City's squad. Sources close to the first team told BBC Sport there is a notable level of concern among players, with some sceptical the appeal will bring a reprieve and others trusting the club's leadership. Most players do not have relegation clauses in their contracts, and their deals are fully guaranteed, meaning they would not take pay cuts if the club lost Premier League status and City would still be entitled to demand transfer fees for any departing players. Agents said players are likely to wait for clarity on sanctions before entering contract negotiations; only Mateo Kovacic, Matheus Nunes, Marcus Bettinelli and Geronimo Rulli have contracts expiring in the next two summers.

The looming punishment also complicates City's transfer plans and player retention, with one agent telling BBC Sport: "Some players want medals, all players want money." City's ability to renew contracts and make signings will depend on the appeal's outcome, and maintaining one of the world's highest wage bills could become harder without Premier League-level income if demotion were to occur. The club maintains its innocence, while the FA and other bodies continue to monitor the case as the appeal process moves forward.

stories.headline: Cowboys acquire Joey Porter Jr. from Steelers in blockbuster trade
body: The Dallas Cowboys acquired cornerback Joey Porter Jr. from the Pittsburgh Steelers on Tuesday, sending a 2027 sixth-round pick and a 2028 second-round pick to Pittsburgh, according to ESPN's Todd Archer and Brooke Pryor. Porter, who has been sidelined with a back injury amid a contract dispute since training camp, will reunite with former Steelers teammates Broderick Jones and George Pickens in Dallas. The Steelers had reportedly been unwilling to offer Porter the extension he sought—widely believed to be in the range of $30 million annually, comparable to the recent deals signed by fellow 2023 cornerbacks Christian Gonzalez ($33.75 million per year) and Devon Witherspoon ($33 million).

The trade comes at a critical juncture for the Cowboys' secondary. Dallas has allowed seven passing touchdowns through three weeks, and cornerback DaRon Bland has surrendered a passer rating of 108.8 in coverage. Cobie Durant missed last week's game with a hamstring injury. Porter recorded 31 pass breakups, three interceptions, and a 57.2 passer rating in coverage over three seasons in Pittsburgh. He is expected to become the Cowboys' clear No. 1 boundary corner once his back injury allows him to take the field.

According to NFL insider Jordan Schultz, the Cowboys are not expected to sign Porter to a new deal, leaving his contract situation unresolved. The cornerback had been seeking an extension averaging around $30 million per year, as reported by Chris Mack of the Kaboly and Mack podcast, but Pittsburgh declined to meet that figure, citing a long-standing organizational policy against negotiating contracts during the regular season and reluctance to guarantee large sums. The Athletic's Mike DeFabo noted that Steelers general manager Omar Khan has a history of letting negotiations linger, and the team had instead extended players such as Keeanu Benton, Nick Herbig, Michael Pittman Jr., Jaylen Warren, and Darnell Washington this offseason.

The trade leaves Pittsburgh with a cornerback duo of Jamel Dean and Asante Samuel Jr. Dean has missed 12 games since 2023, while Samuel has allowed a passer rating of 135.4 and two touchdowns this season. The Steelers, who entered the deal with $11.6 million in cap space and a projected $9.2 million over the limit in 2027, received only draft capital for Porter—no player in return. Bleacher Report gave the Cowboys an 'A' grade for the trade, calling it a 'slam dunk move,' while assigning the Steelers a 'D,' calling the short-term move a 'major blunder.' Porter was graded a 'C,' with the potential benefit of playing for a higher-scoring offense but the same uncertain contract outlook.

stories.headline: Trump expected to name intelligence director Jay Clayton as AI czar
body: President Donald Trump is expected to name Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton as the White House’s artificial intelligence czar, according to a source familiar with the matter. The president teased the move this week and will most likely announce it on social media as early as Friday, the source said. The selection comes after a lengthy meeting with executives of leading technology companies at the White House on Tuesday, which Clayton attended.

Clayton, who oversees the nation’s spy agencies as the director of national intelligence, would take on the AI responsibility alongside his current role. In a CNBC interview Wednesday after the White House AI meeting, Clayton said the Trump administration would be taking a “whole-of-government approach” to regulating the technology. “Superintelligence is a national security issue,” Clayton said, using the term the Trump administration has formally adopted to refer to AI. “That was something that was recognized yesterday by not just the industry leaders, but everybody in the room.”

When reached for a comment about the forthcoming announcement, a White House official said, “Any personnel announcement will be announced directly by the President. Any reporting until then is baseless speculation.”

Trump’s selection of Clayton comes after a groundswell of concern about the consequences associated with AI development following warnings by employees at some of the top AI companies about the technology putting humanity at risk. Trump has largely brushed off these threats, including after his meeting with AI giants, pushing back on calls to implement stronger safety regulations. “I think I’m seeing tremendous self-policing, and they understand that they have to self-police, and it’s very hard for somebody to come outside, get into these. These models are very complex, and again, I believe they’re going to be used for the good,” Trump told reporters at the White House. “And when they’re not, we’re going to be able to nab them. But there’s going to be a tremendous self-policing aspect.”

David Sacks, who now serves as co-chair of the President’s Council of Advisors on Science and Technology, had served as special adviser for AI and Crypto from January 2025 through March of this year. Before he took over the DNI role in August following Senate confirmation, Clayton was the U.S. Attorney for the Southern District of New York. He was chair of the Securities and Exchange Commission during Trump’s first term and previously a partner at top law firm Sullivan & Cromwell.
